photosynthesis.short: How plants, algae and some bacteria use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen. The sugars store the sunlight's energy as chemical energy.

biomass.short: Plant and animal material (wood, crop waste, manure, energy crops) used as fuel. Its energy came from sunlight captured by photosynthesis.

biofuel.short: A liquid or gaseous fuel made from biomass, such as ethanol from sugarcane or corn, or biodiesel from vegetable oils.

anaerobic-digestion.short: Microbes breaking down wet organic matter (manure, food waste, sewage) without oxygen, producing biogas that is mostly methane and carbon dioxide.

gasification.short: Heating biomass with too little oxygen to burn it fully, turning it into a combustible gas of carbon monoxide and hydrogen (syngas).

beccs.term: BECCS (bioenergy with carbon capture and storage)
beccs.short: Burning or fermenting biomass for energy, then capturing the carbon dioxide and storing it underground, so that the carbon the plants took from the air stays out of it.

carbon-debt.short: The extra carbon dioxide released when land is cleared to grow bioenergy crops. It takes years of replacing fossil fuel before the savings repay it.

lifecycle-emissions.short: All the greenhouse gases released to make, run and dispose of an energy source, counted per unit of energy it delivers: farming, fertiliser, transport, processing and land-use change included.

concentrated-solar-power.short: Mirrors focus sunlight to heat a fluid; the heat drives a turbine like a conventional power station. Also called solar thermal electricity.

heliostat.short: A flat, steerable mirror that tracks the Sun so that it always reflects sunlight onto the same fixed target, such as the receiver on top of a tower.

parabolic-trough.short: A long, curved mirror that focuses sunlight onto a pipe running along its focal line. The whole trough turns to follow the Sun.

power-tower.short: A CSP plant in which a field of heliostats reflects sunlight onto a receiver at the top of a central tower. Also called a central receiver.

linear-fresnel.short: Rows of long, nearly flat mirror strips that each tilt to send sunlight onto a fixed pipe above them: a cheaper, flatter cousin of the parabolic trough.

solar-dish.short: A dish-shaped mirror that focuses sunlight onto a point receiver, often driving a small Stirling engine. Reaches the highest concentrations but is built in small units.

concentration-ratio.short: How many times a concentrator multiplies sunlight: the mirror aperture area divided by the receiver area. Troughs reach roughly tens to about a hundred; towers hundreds to about a thousand.

molten-salt.short: A mix of sodium and potassium nitrates, liquid from roughly 240 °C up to about 565 °C, used to carry and store heat in CSP plants.

sensible-heat.short: Heat stored by raising a material's temperature (as opposed to melting it). Stored energy = mass × specific heat × temperature rise.

energy-storage.short: Holding energy now to deliver it later: batteries, pumped hydro, hydrogen, heat. Rated by power (MW, how fast) and energy (MWh, how much).

storage-duration.short: How many hours a store can deliver at its full power: energy capacity (MWh) divided by power rating (MW). A 100 MW / 400 MWh battery is a 4-hour battery.

state-of-charge.short: How full a store is, as energy (MWh) or as a percentage of its capacity.

pumped-storage.short: Two reservoirs at different heights: pump water uphill when power is cheap and plentiful, let it run back down through turbines when it is needed. By energy stored, the largest form of grid storage.

flow-battery.short: A battery whose energy is stored in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks and pumped through a cell stack. Bigger tanks mean more hours of storage.

lithium-ion.short: A rechargeable battery in which lithium ions shuttle between two electrodes. Grid batteries mostly use the LFP (lithium iron phosphate) chemistry; many cars use NMC (nickel manganese cobalt).

electrolysis.short: Using electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen can be stored and later turned back into electricity or used as a fuel.

fuel-cell.short: A device that combines hydrogen with oxygen to make electricity, water and heat directly, without burning.

curtailment.short: Turning down wind or solar output that could have been generated, because the grid cannot use or store it at that moment.

net-load.short: Demand minus the output of wind and solar: what the rest of the grid (hydro, gas, storage, imports) must supply.

duck-curve.short: The shape of net load on a sunny spring day in a grid with lots of solar: a deep midday belly and a steep evening climb as the Sun sets. Named by the California grid operator.

grid-frequency.short: How many times per second alternating current reverses: 50 Hz in most of the world, 60 Hz in North America, parts of South America and parts of Asia. It dips when demand exceeds supply and rises when supply exceeds demand.

inertia.short: The energy stored in the spinning turbines and generators of a grid. It resists sudden changes in frequency, buying a few seconds for reserves to respond.

rocof.short: How fast grid frequency moves after a sudden loss of supply or demand, in hertz per second. Less inertia means a faster change.

hvdc.short: Transmission by direct current at hundreds of kilovolts or more. Loses less energy than alternating current over long distances and under the sea, and links grids that are not synchronised.

interconnector.short: A transmission line or cable linking two grids, often between countries, so each can import when short and export when in surplus.

demand-response.short: Moving or trimming electricity use when the grid is stretched: heating water at noon instead of evening, pausing car charging, industry cutting load for a fee.

grid-forming-inverter.short: An inverter that sets its own voltage and frequency, like a spinning generator does, instead of following the grid's. It can help steady a grid with little spinning inertia.

dispatch.short: Deciding, minute by minute, which power plants and stores run and how hard, so that supply matches demand.

smart-grid.short: A grid with sensors, communications and automatic controls, so that generation, storage and demand can be monitored and coordinated in near real time.

variable-renewable.short: Sources whose output follows the weather and time of day rather than demand, chiefly wind and solar photovoltaics.
